module Whimsy where

import Data.List (nub, sort)

-- A mysterious transformation
enigmatic :: [Int] -> [Int]
enigmatic xs =
  xs
    |> map (* 2)
    |> filter even
    |> nub
    |> sort

-- Custom pipe operator for fun
(|>) :: a -> (a -> b) -> b
x |> f = f x

-- Recursive Fibonacci with memo-ish behavior
fib :: Int -> Int
fib n
  | n < 0     = error "Negative numbers anger the recursion gods"
  | n == 0    = 0
  | n == 1    = 1
  | otherwise = fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2)

-- A lazy infinite stream of weird numbers
weirdStream :: [Int]
weirdStream = [ x * y | x <- [1..], y <- [1..x], x `mod` y == 0 ]

-- Pattern matching just because
describe :: Maybe Int -> String
describe Nothing  = "Nothing to see here"
describe (Just 0) = "Zero, the void"
describe (Just n) = "A number: " ++ show n

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum Entity {
    Warrior { name: String, strength: u32 },
    Mage { name: String, mana: u32 },
    Rogue { name: String, agility: u32 },
}

impl Entity {
    fn power(&self) -> u32 {
        match self {
            Entity::Warrior { strength, .. } => strength * 2,
            Entity::Mage { mana, .. } => mana * 3,
            Entity::Rogue { agility, .. } => agility * 2 + 10,
        }
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        match self {
            Entity::Warrior { name, .. } => name,
            Entity::Mage { name, .. } => name,
            Entity::Rogue { name, .. } => name,
        }
    }
}

fn simulate_battle(entities: &[Entity]) -> HashMap<String, u32> {
    let mut results = HashMap::new();

    for entity in entities {
        println!("{} enters the arena...", entity.name());
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));

        let score = entity.power() + rand::random::<u8>() as u32;
        results.insert(entity.name().to_string(), score);
    }

    results
}

fn main() {
    let party = vec![
        Entity::Warrior {
            name: "Thorin".into(),
            strength: 40,
        },
        Entity::Mage {
            name: "Elora".into(),
            mana: 30,
        },
        Entity::Rogue {
            name: "Shade".into(),
            agility: 25,
        },
    ];

    let results = simulate_battle(&party);

    println!("\nFinal scores:");
    for (name, score) in results {
        println!("{} => {}", name, score);
    }
}

This is plain text (no language)

BibTeX citations

Citations use Pandoc-style [@key] syntax. The plugin processes them after Kramdown renders the Markdown, so they require no special template tags.

A single citation: the spacing effect is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology [@smith2020].

A group citation in one bracket: several authors have discussed this phenomenon in depth [@smith2020; @jones2019].

A book reference is handled the same way [@jones2019]. Conference papers work too [@chen2021].

Suppress the author name with a leading - — useful mid-sentence when the author is already named. As Jones [-@jones2019] argues, the principle generalises broadly.

A References section is automatically appended at the end of this post.

Popup examples

All fields — title, author, date, tags, and abstract:

Researchers studying memory have long relied on spaced repetition as a high-leverage study method.

Title + abstract only — the minimal useful popup:

The concept of emergence appears across physics, biology, and economics.

Title + author + date — no tags or abstract:

Alan Turing laid the theoretical foundations for modern computing.

Title only — the absolute minimum:

See also: Gödel’s incompleteness theorems.

Highlight comments

Unlike popups, highlight comments require no markup at all — any text in the post body is annotatable. Select any phrase in the paragraphs below to open the comment box.

The spacing effect is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology: memories consolidated across distributed practice sessions are retained far longer than those drilled in a single massed block. Spaced repetition software such as Anki exploits this by scheduling each card’s review just before the memory would decay.

Emergence is the phenomenon whereby a system exhibits properties or behaviours that none of its individual parts possess in isolation. A canonical example is consciousness arising from neurons: no single neuron is conscious, yet their collective activity produces subjective experience. Other examples include wetness arising from water molecules, traffic jams from individual drivers, and market prices from individual buyers and sellers.

What the system will not let you annotate:

  • Text inside code spans or fenced code blocks
  • The post title, author line, or tag chips at the top

Anime.js in sidenotes

Footnotes can contain live animations. On desktop each one appears in a sidenote to the right; on mobile it falls back to the standard footnote list. Every script uses querySelectorAll('…')[last] to capture the most recently inserted copy of its container, so the sidenote clone is targeted rather than the original element in the footnotes list.

A rolling wave of five coloured dots2 is the simplest case — animate with stagger and loop. A single SVG ring that draws and erases itself3 shows svg.createDrawable called with a directly captured DOM element, which sidesteps the CSS-selector ID-conflict caveat entirely. A 4 × 4 grid that ripples outward from the centre4 demonstrates stagger with the grid option inside a createTimeline.

Anime.js animations

1 — Staggered wave (animate + stagger + loop)

Nine dots bounce in a wave. Each dot is delayed by 80 ms relative to its neighbour, creating a rolling effect.

2 — SVG line drawing (svg.createDrawable + createTimeline + stagger)

Four concentric circles draw themselves in sequence, then loop. The svg.createDrawable helper exposes a draw property — a "start end" fraction pair that drives stroke-dashoffset automatically.

3 — Grid ripple (stagger with grid + from center)

A 6 × 6 grid of squares scales in from the centre outward, then collapses back, on repeat. stagger accepts a grid: [cols, rows] option that computes each element’s delay based on its 2-D distance from the origin.

TikZ diagrams

These examples use the {% tikz name %}...{% endtikz %} Liquid block tag defined in _plugins/tikz.rb. Each block is compiled to SVG at build time via pdflatex + dvisvgm and cached by content hash in assets/tikz/. Only changed diagrams recompile on subsequent jekyll serve restarts.

1 — Parabola plot

A coordinate-axes plot of $y = x^2$. Wrapped in .block-tikz to centre it at 50% width; the tag itself produces a plain <img> pointing to the compiled SVG.

2 — Finite automaton

A DFA that accepts strings over ${a,b}$ containing at least two $a$’s. The automata and positioning TikZ libraries are already loaded in the plugin’s PREAMBLE, so no extra \usetikzlibrary{} is needed here. Wrapped in .block-tikz large (80% width) because the three-node layout is wider than the parabola.

3 — CSS-animated inline SVG

The inline keyword changes the output from <img> to <div class="tikz-inline" data-tikz-src="…">. On DOMContentLoaded, tikz-loader.js fetches the SVG and injects it into the DOM, making its internal <path> elements reachable by CSS. The spin below is pure CSS — no JavaScript at runtime.

entry.title: Welcome to Jekyll!
entry.content:
You’ll find this post in your _posts directory. Go ahead and edit it and re-build the site to see your changes. You can rebuild the site in many different ways, but the most common way is to run jekyll serve, which launches a web server and auto-regenerates your site when a file is updated.1

Jekyll requires blog post files to be named according to the following format2:

YEAR-MONTH-DAY-title.MARKUP

Where YEAR is a four-digit number, MONTH and DAY are both two-digit numbers, and MARKUP is the file extension representing the format used in the file. After that, include the necessary front matter. Take a look at the source for this post to get an idea about how it works.

Jekyll also offers powerful support for code snippets1:

Check out the Jekyll docs for more info on how to get the most out of Jekyll. File all bugs/feature requests at Jekyll’s GitHub repo. If you have questions, you can ask them on Jekyll Talk.

  1. There’s --livereload flag that’s also cool to use. But I think I’m not ready to look into that just yet. And it should be even longer because why not. We want to wrap, and BAD. ↩ ↩2

  2. whatever. and link. ↩

entry.title: Introducing Tale
entry.content:
Tale is a minimal Jekyll theme curated for storytellers. It is designed and developed by myself for a friend who writes short stories.

Tale features

  • Compatible with GitHub Pages
  • Responsive design (looks just as good on mobile)
  • Syntax highlighting, with the help of Pygments
  • Markdown and HTML text formatting
  • Pagination of posts

Head over to the Example Content post for a showcase of Tale’s text formatting features.

Browser Support

Tale works on most if not all modern browsers, including Chrome, Safari and Firefox 👍🏼

Download or Contribute

Tale is publicly hosted on GitHub, so go ahead and download or fork it at the GitHub repository. If you spot any bugs or have any suggestions, feel free to create an issue or make a pull request.

Thanks for checking out Tale!
